title: The gopis and the learned messenger
hookLine: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar
carry: bhakti needs two: a lover and a beloved

lines: I DON'T WANT TO BECOME SUGAR.
cards: In Calcutta, the mystic Ramakrishna, whose student Vivekananda you met a few weeks ago, used to repeat a line from an old Bengali devotional song.
People asked him about merging into God, becoming one with the absolute, and he'd answer, more or less: I don't want to become sugar. I want to taste sugar. It's a joke, and an argument.
If you become the sugar, who's left to enjoy the sweetness?

teach.b: This is the heart of bhakti, devotion, and the devotional schools make their case in that one line.
Love, they say, needs two: a lover and a beloved, someone to give and someone to receive, someone to sing and someone to hear.
Take away the difference, and you may have peace, or bliss, but not love the way a mother loves a child, or a friend a friend. The Bhagavata Purana tells a story about this.

teach.h: THE GOPIS WANT KRISHNA, NOT A THEORY.
teach.b: Krishna has left the village where he grew up, and the cowherd women who loved him, the gopis, are heartbroken. He sends his friend Uddhava, a learned man, to comfort them, and Uddhava comforts them with philosophy.
Krishna is everywhere, he says; he's the self of all; you're never really apart from him. The gopis answer, paraphrased: that's lovely. We want Krishna.
Not the self of all. Him. His flute, his laugh, his face.

Uddhava, humbled, says he'd gladly be a bush or a creeper in their village, just to be touched by the dust of their feet. Other teachers explored the ground between. Nimbarka taught difference and non-difference at once.
In Bengal, Chaitanya's followers called it inconceivable: one with God and different from God, both, beyond what the mind can hold. Now, fairly.

Advaita teachers honor devotion too, as you heard with Bhaja Govindam, and some of them say love, fully ripened, dissolves into oneness. The devotional schools say love, fully ripened, stays two and grows forever.
Hindus hold both, side by side.

teach.h: BHAKTI NEEDS TWO: A LOVER AND A BELOVED.

how: In Vaishnava devotional traditions, teachers often explain that bhakti depends on the relationship between the devotee and God, and the gopis' love for Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana is held up as its model.

the cowherd women who loved Krishna

games.q: love needs two — tap the pairs.

s: the gopis were comforted by Uddhava's philosophy
they answered: we want Krishna himself. Uddhava went home humbled.
they honor it; some say love, fully ripened, dissolves into oneness.
Ramakrishna's sugar line comes from a Bengali devotional song
he often repeated it from an older song, as the devotee's answer to merging into God.

games.q: you're one of the gopis. Uddhava tells you Krishna is the self of all, so you're never really apart from him. what do you say?
games.why: they want Krishna himself, not an idea. Uddhava, the learned man, wished he could be a bush or a creeper in their village.

practice: Hindus often offer food to God before they eat, then receive it back as prasad, a gift. Try it with something nearby, a sip of tea, a raisin, a square of chocolate, or remember one.
Hold it a moment and offer it in your heart to God, or simply say thank you. Then taste it slowly, and notice two things: the sweetness, and the one enjoying it. That's Ramakrishna's sugar.

wordCard.voice: Gopis, the cowherd women who loved Krishna. Love needs a lover and a beloved; to taste sugar, you can't become it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: achintya (inconceivable) + bheda-abheda (difference and non-difference): Chaitanya's school's view of God and soul.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti needs two, a lover and a beloved. Someone has to be there to taste the sugar. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: sayings of Ramakrishna as recorded by his disciples (the sugar image, echoing Ramprasad Sen)
Nimbarka (dvaitadvaita) and the Gaudiya school of Chaitanya (acintya-bhedabheda)
